Partial cubes are graphs that can be embedded isometrically into hypercubes—that is, the distance between any two vertices is preserved under the embedding. Their study relies heavily on semicubes and on the relations introduced by Djoković and Winkler, which provide fundamental tools for analyzing the edge and metric structure of these graphs.

Using these concepts, one can characterize both bipartite graphs and partial cubes of arbitrary dimension. The paper develops several new characterizations while also offering alternative proofs of established results, thereby providing a unified perspective on the theory.

The paper further examines constructive operations, including Cartesian products, pasting, expansion, and contraction. These operations generate new partial cubes from existing ones and facilitate the calculation of two important embedding parameters: isometric dimension, which concerns embeddings into hypercubes, and lattice dimension, which concerns embeddings into integer lattices. Together, these structural and constructive approaches deepen the understanding of partial cubes and their metric properties.

The paper investigates the structure of bipartite graphs and partial cubes through the metric properties of their edges and vertex sets. A partial cube is a graph that admits an isometric embedding into a hypercube, meaning that graph distances are preserved by the embedding. Central to the analysis are semicubes: for an oriented edge \(ab\), the corresponding semicube consists of all vertices that are closer to \(a\) than to \(b\). In bipartite graphs, the two semicubes associated with an edge partition the vertex set. Their convexity provides an effective criterion for deciding whether a connected graph is a partial cube.

The study also examines Djoković’s and Winkler’s relations on the edge set. These relations identify edges that represent the same coordinate direction in a hypercube embedding. Their definitions and properties are compared, and their behavior in bipartite graphs is used to obtain characterizations of partial cubes. In particular, the paper relates the transitivity and equivalence classes of these relations to the convexity of semicubes and to the existence of isometric hypercube embeddings. This approach yields new proofs and alternative formulations of several fundamental results concerning partial cubes.

A further part of the paper focuses on graph operations that preserve partial-cube structure. Cartesian products are considered as a basic method for combining graphs while retaining their metric properties. The treatment explains how semicubes and edge-equivalence classes behave under Cartesian multiplication and how embeddings of the factors can be combined to produce an embedding of the product. Pasting operations are also studied, with attention paid to the conditions under which two partial cubes can be joined along a common subgraph without destroying convexity or distance preservation.

Expansion and contraction provide additional ways to construct and simplify partial cubes. An expansion replaces part of a graph by two suitably connected copies, introducing a new family of parallel edges and, correspondingly, a new hypercube coordinate. Contraction reverses this process by collapsing the edges of an appropriate equivalence class. The paper describes these operations in terms of semicubes and Djoković–Winkler classes, proves that the relevant constructions preserve the partial-cube property, and shows how they can be used to generate new examples from known graphs. These results also clarify the recursive structure of finite partial cubes.

Finally, the paper determines the dimensions of the finite partial cubes obtained through these constructions. The isometric dimension is the smallest dimension of a hypercube into which the graph embeds isometrically; it is governed by the number of distinct Djoković–Winkler equivalence classes of edges. The lattice dimension is the smallest integer \(d\) for which the graph admits an isometric embedding into the integer lattice \(\mathbb{Z}^{d}\) with its standard graph metric. By tracing the effects of Cartesian products, pasting, expansion, and contraction on semicubes and edge classes, the paper derives the isometric and lattice dimensions of the resulting graphs. Together, these results provide both structural characterizations of partial cubes and practical tools for constructing them and computing their embedding dimensions.

## Partial Cube Structures and the Djoković Relation

In graph theory, **partial cubes** are structures that can be embedded isometrically into a hypercube. This means that vertices of a partial cube can be represented by binary vectors so that the graph distance between any two vertices equals their Hamming distance—the number of coordinates in which the vectors differ. Trees, even cycles, and many graphs arising from chemical structures are important examples of partial cubes.

A fundamental tool for studying these graphs is the **Djoković relation**, introduced by Dragomir Ž. Djoković. For two edges \(e=xy\) and \(f=uv\) of a connected graph, the relation is defined by

\[
e \,\Theta\, f
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
d(x,u)+d(y,v)\neq d(x,v)+d(y,u),
\]

where \(d\) denotes the shortest-path distance.

In a hypercube, two edges are related precisely when they correspond to a change in the same coordinate. Thus, the equivalence classes of the Djoković relation identify the different “directions” or dimensions of the cube. For partial cubes, the relation is transitive and therefore partitions the edge set into classes known as **\(\Theta\)-classes**.

Each \(\Theta\)-class determines a cut of the graph into two convex vertex subsets. Removing all edges in one class separates the graph into two components, analogous to dividing a hypercube according to whether a selected coordinate is \(0\) or \(1\). These cuts reveal the hidden cubical structure of the graph and make it possible to construct an isometric binary labeling of its vertices.

The Djoković relation also provides a useful characterization: a connected graph is a partial cube if and only if it is bipartite and the relation \(\Theta\) is transitive. Consequently, the relation is important both theoretically and algorithmically. It can be used to recognize partial cubes, calculate their isometric dimension, analyze convex substructures, and study networks in which graph distance must be preserved exactly.

This paper examines their structure through semicubes and two fundamental edge relations: Djoković’s relation and Winkler’s relation. We describe how these relations capture the hypercube-like organization of a graph’s edge set and review their role in characterizing partial cubes, particularly through convexity properties of semicubes and equivalence classes of edges. Building on these characterizations, we develop and compare methods for constructing partial cubes, including expansion-based operations, Cartesian products, and procedures derived from compatible semicube systems. We establish conditions under which these constructions preserve isometric embeddability and show how the associated edge classes determine hypercube coordinates. The resulting framework unifies structural and constructive perspectives on partial cubes and provides practical tools for recognizing, generating, and analyzing this important class of graphs.

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize a graph theory paper that characterizes bipartite graphs and partial cubes and studies Cartesian products, pasting, expansion, and contraction.
counterfactuals.output:
The paper develops structural characterizations of **bipartite graphs** and **partial cubes**—graphs that admit an isometric embedding into a hypercube—using graph distances and edge equivalence relations.

Its central idea is that edges can be grouped according to the cuts they induce. In a partial cube, each such edge class separates the graph into two convex “halfspaces.” This yields the standard characterization: a connected graph is a partial cube precisely when it is bipartite and the Djoković–Winkler relation on edges behaves transitively, equivalently when the corresponding semicubes are convex.

The paper then studies how this structure interacts with several graph operations:

- **Cartesian products:** Partial cubes are closed under Cartesian product. The edge classes of the product come directly from the factors, matching the coordinate structure of hypercubes.
- **Pasting:** Under suitable convexity or compatibility conditions, partial cubes may be glued along common subgraphs while preserving their isometric-hypercube structure.
- **Expansion:** Splitting a graph along overlapping convex pieces creates a new coordinate, or edge class. Expansions preserve partial cubes and provide a constructive description: every finite partial cube can be obtained from a single vertex by successive suitable expansions.
- **Contraction:** Contracting all edges in one coordinate class removes that hypercube coordinate and produces a smaller partial cube. Contraction is thus the inverse of expansion.

Overall, the paper connects three viewpoints on partial cubes: **metric characterizations**, **convex cuts and edge classes**, and **constructive operations**. It shows that partial cubes are not merely subgraphs of hypercubes but form a robust graph class whose geometry can be built up, decomposed, and analyzed coordinate by coordinate.

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a concise academic overview of research on partial cubes, including new characterizations, construction operations, and calculations of isometric and lattice dimensions.
counterfactuals.output:
### Overview

A **partial cube** is a graph that admits an isometric embedding into a hypercube: vertices can be labelled by binary vectors so that graph distance equals Hamming distance. Partial cubes include trees, median graphs, even cycles, benzenoid graphs, and cover graphs of several classes of ordered structures.

A fundamental characterization uses the **Djoković–Winkler relation** \(\Theta\) on edges. For edges \(uv\) and \(xy\),
\[
uv\mathrel{\Theta}xy
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
d(u,x)+d(v,y)\ne d(u,y)+d(v,x).
\]
A connected graph is a partial cube precisely when it is bipartite and \(\Theta\) is transitive, hence an equivalence relation. Equivalently, for every edge \(uv\), the two semicubes
\[
W_{uv}=\{x:d(x,u)<d(x,v)\},\qquad W_{vu}=V(G)\setminus W_{uv}
\]
are convex. These results connect partial cubes with convex split systems, well-graded set families, media, and median-type structures. More recent characterizations often emphasize compatibility among convex cuts, gated subgraphs, or the behavior of \(\Theta\)-classes under contraction.

### Construction operations

The principal constructive operation is **expansion**. Roughly, an isometric cover by two overlapping subgraphs is separated into two copies of the overlap, with corresponding vertices joined by a matching. Under the standard expansion conditions, the resulting graph remains a partial cube and gains one \(\Theta\)-class. Conversely, contracting any \(\Theta\)-class preserves the partial-cube property. Consequently, every finite partial cube can be generated from a single vertex by successive expansions.

Important restricted forms include convex, peripheral, and gated expansions. Partial cubes are also closed under Cartesian products; their \(\Theta\)-classes are inherited from the factors. Gated amalgamation and related gluing operations provide further constructions for median graphs and other structured subclasses.

### Isometric and lattice dimensions

For a finite partial cube \(G\), the **isometric dimension**
\[
\operatorname{idim}(G)
\]
is the least \(q\) such that \(G\) embeds isometrically into the hypercube \(Q_q\). It is exactly the number of \(\Theta\)-classes:
\[
\operatorname{idim}(G)=|E(G)/\Theta|.
\]
A canonical embedding assigns one binary coordinate to each convex split induced by a \(\Theta\)-class.

The **lattice dimension** \(\operatorname{ldim}(G)\) is the least \(d\) for which \(G\) embeds isometrically into the integer lattice \(\mathbb Z^d\) with the \(L_1\) metric. If \(q=\operatorname{idim}(G)\), form the semicube graph whose vertices are the \(2q\) semicubes and whose edges join disjoint, noncomplementary semicubes. If \(\nu\) is the size of a maximum matching in this graph, then
\[
\operatorname{ldim}(G)=q-\nu.
\]
The matching identifies hypercube cuts that can be arranged as successive thresholds of one lattice coordinate. Thus both dimensions are computable combinatorially: first determine the \(\Theta\)-classes, then solve a maximum-matching problem. For example, \(Q_q\) has both dimensions \(q\), while a tree with \(m\) leaves has isometric dimension \(|E|\) and lattice dimension \(\lceil m/2\rceil\).
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a journal-style abstract explaining how Cartesian products, pasting, expansions, and contractions can construct finite partial cubes and determine their isometric and lattice dimensions.
counterfactuals.output: **Abstract.** We present a constructive framework for finite partial cubes based on four operations: Cartesian products, isometric pasting, expansions, and contractions. Starting from elementary factors, Cartesian products combine partial cubes while preserving graph distances, with both isometric dimension and lattice dimension behaving additively. Compatible pastings along convex or gated subgraphs permit larger partial cubes to be assembled while identifying shared distance coordinates. Expansions introduce new Djoković–Winkler \(\Theta\)-classes by splitting a graph along an appropriate convex cover, whereas contraction of a \(\Theta\)-class provides the inverse reduction and supports inductive decompositions to a single vertex. This viewpoint yields dimension algorithms intrinsic to the construction. The isometric dimension—the minimum dimension of a hypercube containing the graph isometrically—is the number of \(\Theta\)-classes and can therefore be updated directly under each operation. The lattice dimension—the minimum \(d\) admitting an isometric embedding into \(\mathbb Z^d\) with the \(\ell_1\) metric—is obtained by determining which \(\Theta\)-classes can be consistently placed on the same lattice axis; equivalently, it may be computed from an optimal matching or path-cover formulation in the associated semicube graph. Thus products, pastings, expansions, and contractions provide both a structural generation scheme for finite partial cubes and a unified method for constructing embeddings and determining their hypercube and integer-lattice dimensions.
